title: 7 players to make worlds debut as Canadian women's hockey team looks to youth
summary: The Canadian women's hockey team will take a young roster to the world championship in Denmark next month. It will be the first major tournament since the Canadians lost the Olympic final to the U.S.…

image.caption: Montreal Victoire forward Jessie Eldridge has played her way on to the Canadian women's national team's world-championship roster. The Canadians will look to reclaim gold in Denmark, beginning on Nov. 6. (Jon Blacker/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: PWHL

The Canadian women's hockey team will take a young roster to the world championship in Denmark next month. It will be the first major tournament since the Canadians lost the Olympic final to the U.S. in February.
Shift comes after Canada lost to U.S. at Olympics, last year's world championship

When the Canadians arrive in Denmark in the coming weeks to try to reclaim the women's hockey world championship, it will be with a remarkably different roster than the one that lined up at the Olympics this past February.
That veteran-laden roster finished second to the Americans, after a hard-fought gold-medal game went into overtime.

Zoom further out, and you'll see a Canadian team that failed to beat the Americans over eight straight matchups. At times, the Canadians looked slower and less connected than the Americans, who embraced young talent over the last four years.
But if the roster for the first major tournament of a new Olympic quad is any indication, things are changing on Team Canada.

Seven players will make their world championship debut next month in Denmark, which will host the world championship from Nov. 6 to 16. The roster was announced on Monday, after a training camp in Quebec City earlier this month.

blocks.text: "There is a great sense of energy, hunger and determination within this group," head coach Kori Cheverie said in a statement. "We’re looking forward to building on that momentum as we prepare to compete in Denmark.”

The roster includes several players who have made a mark at the Under-18 level, including 18-year-old Rosalie Tremblay (University of Wisconsin), 18-year-old Hayley McDonald (Ohio State University), and 19-year-old Sara Manness (Clarkson University).
Nineteen-year-old defender Chloe Primerano is one of six college players who will suit up for Canada at the upcoming women's world championship. (Melissa Majchrzak/The Associated Press)

Three other collegiate players, 19-year-old Chloe Primerano (University of Minnesota), 20-year-old Caitlin Kraemer (University of Minnesota Duluth) and 23-year-old Ève Gascon (University of Minnesota Duluth) return for their second world championship.
Gascon has had a phenomenal start to her NCAA season, only allowing two goals in five games so far. She's posted four shutouts.

In some cases, players were selected for their potential at the next level. But in order to bring that potential out, young players need a chance to show what they can do, new Canadian GM Danièle Sauvageau told reporters on Monday.
"They earned their place to be able to show what they could do at the international level," Sauvageau said.
PWHL performance played a role
Other players forced their way on to the team with stellar performances in the PWHL, including Ottawa Charge forward Rebecca Leslie and the Montreal Victoire's Jessie Eldridge.

It will be Eldridge's first world-championship appearance since 2022, despite being one of the top offensive producers in the PWHL. Only three players have scored more goals than Eldridge since the league launched in 2024.

blocks.text: Leslie will make her world championship debut, after previous stints with the senior national team at the Rivalry Series.
The Ottawa native scored 14 goals in 30 regular-season games for the Charge last season, tying Eldridge for second in the league, behind Minnesota's Kelly Pannek.

But it wasn't just Leslie's ability to score goals that put her on Hockey Canada's radar. It was her performance over the last two seasons during the playoffs, where she helped take the Charge to back-to-back appearances in the Walter Cup final.
The hope is that her play during the grit and intensity of the PWHL playoffs will translate to best-on-best at the international level.

blocks.text: "What we’ve seen at the camp was enough to make us believe that she could continue to have the same performance at the international level," Sauvageau said.
Several veterans to miss tournament

Only 13 members of the Olympic team were named to the roster. Several notable veterans will not be there, including captain Marie-Philip Poulin, who had major knee surgery in July. It's not clear when Poulin might be able to return to the ice.
Even though she can't play, Poulin made an appearance at training camp for a team dinner, and has spoken to young players.

"It’s hard for her," Sauvageau said about Poulin's absence. "It’s hard for us not having her around. But she is still the captain of Team Canada. The role that she’s playing is the role that she wants to play, and she’s there and she’s obviously one phone call away."
Also absent is Vancouver Goldeneyes forward Sarah Nurse, who missed training camp with back issues, and Toronto Sceptres forward Blayre Turnbull, who is pregnant.

With all the change, the Canadian team will head into a world championship with only one player, Renata Fast, who wore a letter last season. Alternate captains and long-time Team Canada stalwarts Jocelyne Larocque and Brianne Jenner attended training camp, but were not named to the team.
Sauvageau said there are other players on the team who could be wearing a letter.
"We believe we have enough leadership," she said. "Leadership is never an end, either. What we used to do yesterday, we cannot continue to do it tomorrow."

The world championship roster is the first look at the team's identity under the new leadership group, led by Sauvageau and Cheverie, who took over for former GM Gina Kingsbury and former head coach Troy Ryan over the summer.

When talking about the team's identity, Sauvageau described the ideal team as fast and connected, and able to score plenty of goals. That's something Canada has struggled to do against the U.S. in particular over the last year.
Montreal Victoire head coach Kori Cheverie was named head coach of the Canadian women's national team this past summer. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)
Cheverie's coaching staff will also include Caroline Ouellette (Montreal Victoire), Alison Domenico (University of Ottawa), and Kris Sparre (PWHL Hamilton).
Canada and the U.S. will play two exhibition games ahead of the world championship. The first will be on Oct. 28 in Windsor, Ont., followed by a game in Plymouth, Mich. on Oct. 30.
PWHL training camps will open on Nov. 18.
